one_liner: Alternative Python interpreter with a meta-tracing JIT; runs pure-Python CPU-bound code 1.5-42x faster than CPython.
what_it_does: PyPy is a complete Python implementation (PyPy2.7, PyPy3.11 and, since v8.0.0, a beta PyPy3.12) that runs unmodified Python source: you replace `python3 app.py` with `pypy3 app.py`. Pure-Python packages work as-is; CPython C extensions load through the cpyext compatibility layer, and cffi is the recommended way to call C. It is a standalone interpreter, not a library you link into a C++ program.
how_it_is_fast: The interpreter is written in RPython, and the RPython toolchain generates a meta-tracing JIT from it: hot loops are recorded as linear traces of interpreter operations, then optimised (guards, constant folding, allocation removal of short-lived objects via escape analysis) and compiled to machine code. Object-model tricks the JIT exploits include map dicts (hidden-class style instance layouts), dict and list strategies that store unboxed ints or floats, and method caching. Memory management is incminimark, an incremental generational moving GC with bump-pointer nursery allocation instead of reference counting.
when_to_use: Long-running pure-Python CPU-bound code (interpreters, parsers, simulations, numeric loops over lists or array.array): kostya matmul ran 42x and the Brainfuck interpreter 6.5x faster than CPython 3.14.6.
Batch jobs and services that run for seconds or longer, so the JIT warm-up is amortised; the PyPy FAQ says even simple comparisons should run at least one second.
Code that allocates many small short-lived objects in hot loops, where allocation removal and the nursery GC pay off.
Projects whose native dependencies use cffi or are pure Python, so nothing goes through cpyext.
when_not_to_use: Short scripts, CLI tools and test suites: the FAQ warns of a very high JIT warm-up cost and that tests run once and are a bad case for JIT compilers.
Workloads dominated by C-implemented library calls: kostya base64 is slower on PyPy (3.534 s vs 3.099 s for CPython), and the FAQ notes PyPy only speeds up code written in Python.
Stacks built on CPython C extensions (NumPy, pandas, many binary wheels): cpyext emulates refcounting and is documented as slow, and wheel availability for PyPy lags.
Memory-constrained deployments: base RSS is about 60 MiB versus about 11 MiB for CPython in the kostya tables.
Code that needs Python 3.13+ features or a free-threaded build: PyPy tracks 3.11 (last supported in 8.0.x) and 3.12 (beta), and keeps a GIL.

integration.form: standalone interpreter binary (release tarballs, distro packages); not a library
integration.dependencies: none for the release binaries (glibc 2.28+ for Linux tarballs since v8.0.0); building from source needs a Python 2.7 host (PyPy2.7 recommended) with cffi, a C compiler, libffi, zlib, bzip2 and other dev packages
integration.min_toolchain: Runs Python 2.7, 3.11 or 3.12 (beta) code; a source translation takes about 20 minutes and at least 6 GB RAM on 64-bit per pypy/doc/build.rst
integration.platforms: Binaries for x86-64 and x86-32 Linux, macOS x86-64 and arm64, Windows 64-bit, aarch64 Linux; PPC64 (BE and LE), ARM32, RISC-V RV64IMAFD and s390x Linux supported without official binaries
integration.thread_safety: Has a GIL like default CPython; threads do not run Python code in parallel (the STM no-GIL variant is experimental and not shipped).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: pure-Python code runs unchanged, but the language version lags CPython, C extensions go through slower cpyext, and GC semantics differ (no refcounting)

gotchas: No reference counting: files and sockets are not closed when they go out of scope (written data can sit in buffers), memoryviews are not released promptly, and sys.getrefcount does not exist; use with-blocks and explicit close().
The GitHub default branch `main` is the Python 2.7 interpreter (CPYTHON_VERSION 2.7.18); the Python 3 interpreters live on the py3.11 and py3.12 branches.

Some operations are much slower than CPython: `del` of a module or class attribute (documented), closures with keyword-only defaults (#5438 open), list copying (#5315 open); 229 issues match 'slower than CPython', many fixed (e.g. bytearray(n) 28x slower, #5567).

Benchmark harness note: kostya/benchmarks times only the region between in-process start/stop notifications, excluding interpreter startup, file loading and a short self-test that runs the same code path, which helps PyPy on the sub-second JSON and primes tests; plb2 timed wall clock with startup, but its slow implementations (CPython included) were timed once with `time` rather than hyperfine. All five kostya scripts verify their output before timing; no correctness bug was found.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick PyPy over Codon, Cython or mypyc when you want to keep running ordinary, untyped Python source unchanged rather than compile a typed subset or an extension module; pick it over GraalPy when you want the faster and lighter runtime, since GraalPy mostly lost to PyPy3 in the independent kostya/jit-benchmarks suite.
verified_claims_summary: kostya/benchmarks ran the same Python files under PyPy 7.3.23 (Python 3.11.15) and Debian CPython 3.14.6 in Docker on an Intel Xeon E-2324G, reporting medians: Brainfuck bench.b 9.398 s vs 61.009 s (6.5x), matmul n=1500 3.263 s vs 136.267 s (42x), primes 0.617 s vs 1.725 s (2.8x), JSON 0.606 s vs 0.936 s (1.5x), while base64 was slower (3.534 s vs 3.099 s); ratios derived from page data. attractivechaos/plb2 on an Apple M1 MacBook Pro measured PyPy 7.3.14 against CPython 3.11.7 at 6.91 vs 159.97 s (nqueen, 23x), 4.89 vs 117.81 s (matmul, 24x), 8.82 vs 52.88 s (sudoku, 6.0x) and 6.27 vs 42.84 s (bedcov, 6.8x), derived from page data.
status_note: Very active (last commit 2026-10-05; v8.0.0 released 2026-09 with Python 3.12 beta and cp312-abi3 groundwork, v8.0.1 bug-fix release in preparation), MIT-licensed core with PSF-licensed lib-python, and installable as a binary, so adoption costs a runtime swap rather than a build.
